source.title: Cyber for AI at SemEval-2025 Task 4: Forgotten but Not Lost: The Balancing Act of Selective Unlearning in Large Language Models

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates several unlearning methods on forget-set metrics and general capability, but does not test recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports outcomes for unlearning methods on the task aggregate, MIA score, and MMLU. These bear on the unlearning and utility portions of version A, but the measures do not directly report targeted-knowledge accuracy after an attack. Fine-tuning recovery attacks, activation-direction ablation, quantization recovery, and prompting-only recovery are not tested. Cited related work is not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: This is a SemEval-2025 Task 4 unlearning submission on OLMo 1B and 7B. Most results report its own methods' scores (task aggregate, MIA score, MMLU) with no recovery attacks and no targeted-knowledge accuracy, so they cannot show version A. One reported result does bear on B. On the 7B model (4-bit LoRA), one retain-set gradient-descent epoch after strong gradient-ascent unlearning returned the MIA score to 0 and MMLU to about 0.51. The authors describe this as reinstating the model 'alike the original' (Section 4, Table 9). This is retain-set fine-tuning undoing unlearning, measured only through the MIA score.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude GDf→GA worked best for 7B and retain-set gradient descent for 1B, with Xavier init nearly matching the latter. They stress the forgetting/retention/utility tradeoff and dependence on model scale and data. They do not frame the retain-set reversal as a robustness failure.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates task-specific gradient-based and initialization methods on SemEval Task 4 models and data; it does not evaluate the recovery attacks named in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that learning rate and weight decay strongly affect gradient-ascent unlearning, and that results depend substantially on model scale and training configuration.
record.problems: No recovery attacks are evaluated. MIA and the task aggregate are indirect or combined measures rather than separate targeted-knowledge accuracy after an attack. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The 7B experiments use a 4-bit PEFT configuration.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed configuration rows and the full epoch sweep in Tables 8 and 9 are not separately extracted; the summary results in Tables 3 and 4 capture the principal method outcomes. Overall aggregate scores and test-set scores are omitted because they do not separately measure targeted forgetting or general capability.

untested.parts: Targeted-knowledge accuracy relative to chance, and whether simple attacks recover the forgotten data.
Relearning on loosely related data or on a subset of the forget set. Recovery is measured only through the MIA score, not through forget-set accuracy, and only on the 7B LoRA model.
Not tested as an attack. 4-bit quantization is used only as the 7B training configuration.

missing.what: GA (LR 2e-6, E=10) on 7B, then 1 GD epoch on the retain set (LR 2e-6). MIA goes 0.865→0 and MMLU 0.284→0.511, i.e. the unlearning effect is undone.
GDf→GA model (MIA 0.982) followed by one GD epoch at LR 2e-8. MIA returns to 0 and MMLU to 0.511/0.513, 'reinstated it alike the original'.
missing.locator: Section 4 'Gradient difference followed by Gradient difference'; Table 9 GDf->GDf rows

record.verdict_notes: Task aggregate is a harmonic mean over 12 scores and is 0 for almost every method, including the original model, so it carries no information. The MIA score (1−|AUC−0.5|·2) is ambiguous in direction, and the authors' reading of values near 1 as 'over-unlearning' is unusual. The B verdict is weak evidence: it rests on the MIA score and MMLU only, in a 4-bit LoRA setup. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Whether simple attacks recover the targeted knowledge; direct targeted-knowledge accuracy relative to chance is not separately reported.
Recovery by fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten examples.
Recovery by activation-direction ablation or evidence that unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
Recovery by rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
A newer method's resistance to the attacks above.

relationships.condition: 7B OLMo-Instruct, 4-bit LoRA, gradient-ascent unlearning followed by 1 retain-set gradient-descent epoch (LR 2e-6 or 2e-8)
relationships.reason: Text-based; no row records it (see missing). After gradient-ascent unlearning (MIA 0.865/0.982), one retain-set epoch returned the MIA score to 0, the original's value, and MMLU to 0.511–0.513. The authors say this 'reinstated it alike the original'. Caveat: an MIA score of 0 only means members are fully separable, and forget accuracy is not reported.
relationships.display_finding: One retained-data epoch returned MIA scores from 0.865/0.982 to the original 0 and MMLU to 0.511–0.513; this establishes member separability rather than forgotten-answer recovery.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.reason: MMLU average accuracy is 0.284 versus 0.512 for the original model, and the authors say it almost halved; see r16.
